— Conflicting opinions and research outcomes
Evidence clusters into two incompatible positions: some sources claim Neanderthals had larger absolute brain size than modern humans, while others argue that when comparing contemporary groups or correcting for body size, brain sizes were similar or that Neanderthals devoted more neural tissue to vision and body control, leaving less for higher cognition.

Some sources report that Neanderthals had larger brains than modern humans in absolute terms, with averages around 1500–1600 cc versus modern human averages, and describe their endocasts as bigger and differently shaped. Other sources, however, find that raw volumes are nearly identical and that after correcting for larger Neanderthal body size, the brain volume available for higher cognition is smaller than in modern humans. A third set of sources emphasizes that fossil Neanderthals and modern humans from the same period had similar brain sizes and that Neanderthal brains were organized differently, with relatively larger visual and somatic regions.
